analysis.one_liner: Caps US prescription drug prices at the lowest price charged in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the Senate Health Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to set a yearly maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest list price charged for that drug in 12 other developed countries (Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK). No drug could be sold above that price to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, the VA, federal employees' insurance, the Indian Health Service — or to anyone else in America, insured or not. Manufacturers that charge more would owe a civil penalty, with the money sent to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans who buy prescription drugs. Today Americans often pay several times what people in other developed countries pay for the same drug; this bill would make the lowest of those international prices the legal ceiling for everyone in the US, including people without insurance and people with private coverage. It would also cut federal spending on drugs under Medicare, Medicaid, and other government programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who fill prescriptions in the US

how_it_helps.text: Sets an annual reference price for every drug at the lowest retail list price found among 12 reference countries, and bans selling above that price in Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service-funded care.

Requires manufacturers to offer every drug at the reference price to all individuals — including the uninsured and people with private or employer coverage — so the price cap reaches beyond government programs to the whole market.

Imposes a civil penalty of five times the excess revenue a manufacturer collects over the reference price on federal program sales, and directs all collected penalties to NIH for drug research and development.

The cap applies to brand-name and generic drugs alike, and applies when pricing data from at least 3 reference countries is unavailable by having the Secretary judge the drug's therapeutic value, development costs, and patient access.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US prices for drugs sold anywhere in the country would be capped at levels similar to what they charge abroad. Investors in those companies would absorb the reduction in US drug revenue. If companies earn less on new drugs, some future drug development could be scaled back or delayed.

drawbacks.text: International reference pricing could reduce manufacturers' incentive to develop new drugs, since the US is the largest source of their profits, and companies might delay or skip launching new drugs in the US or raise prices in the reference countries in response.

The penalty formula is tied to sales under the federal programs listed in the bill, so enforcement strength depends on how the Secretary calculates and applies the reference prices, including where fewer than 3 countries have usable pricing data and the price is set by the Secretary's own judgment call.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans who pay far more than people in peer countries for the same medicines, the benefit is large and immediate. The main trade-off is long-run: lower US drug revenue could slow some new drug development. Whether that trade-off is worth it is the core argument over international reference pricing, and this bill takes the side of paying less now. The bill gives the Secretary significant discretion in setting prices where international data is thin, which is a real design risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the End Price Gouging for Medications Act on May 14, 2025, with Sens. Welch, Sanders, and Durbin as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on May 14, 2025, and no further action appears in the record since then.
Three senators have cosponsored the bill: two Democrats and one Independent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers are better off so far: the price cap has not advanced and their current US pricing is unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, whose prices stay as-is

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap drug prices at the lowest international price and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Peter Welch, Bernie Sanders, and Ron Wyden/Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred to the committee on May 14, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research industry
against.role: Major drug manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed international reference pricing as a threat to US drug revenue; no industry opposition to this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all three cosponsors are Democrats or an Independent, and no Republican has signed on; no vote has occurred, so the partisan split on the floor is unknown.

industries.note: Their US list prices — often multiples of what the same drugs sell for in peer countries — would be legally capped at the lowest international price, for government programs and for every purchaser including the uninsured. This is the interest the bill is written against: cheaper drugs for the public mean lower revenue for the industry.

Generic prices are also capped, but generics are typically already far cheaper than reference prices, so the practical effect is small; cheaper drugs across the board would expand volume for low-cost producers.
Because the cap applies to group health plans and individual coverage, employer plans and private insurers would pay the reference price for drugs, lowering their drug spending.

analysis.trajectory: With three cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action more than half a year after referral, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress. It would need a HELP Committee hearing and markup and then floor time, none of which has been scheduled.
